brief.question: What were the main debates in the Australian parliament in 2011, and what positions did members and parties take? Debates that year included The carbon price, Live cattle exports, The Queensland floods and Pokie reform.
brief.answer:
The carbon price dominated the Australian parliament in 2011, with the government introducing the Clean Energy Bill 2011 to impose a tax starting at $23 per tonne on the country’s 500 largest polluters. Government and Greens senators defended the policy as the most cost-effective way to cut emissions, citing support from 13 prominent economists and arguing that revenue would compensate nine out of ten households and fund clean energy investment. Opposition senators and speakers countered that the tax broke Prime Minister Julia Gillard’s election promise, would raise costs, cost jobs, and shift emissions overseas, noting that countries like Canada and the US were not adopting similar measures. One opposition senator accused the “Gillard-Brown Labor-Green government” of being “dictatorial” for gagging debate, while a government speaker highlighted that there had been around 250 questions and over 15 separate MPI debates on carbon pricing that year alone.

Live cattle exports also sparked fierce argument after footage showed Australian cattle being mistreated in Indonesian abattoirs. The government suspended exports to Indonesia until animal welfare standards were established, a move supported by government senators. Opposition senators, including Senator Joyce, called the blanket suspension a “disaster,” citing a failure to consult Western Australia, the Northern Territory, Queensland, and Indonesia, and criticised Foreign Minister Kevin Rudd for being absent from trade negotiations. A bill to end all live exports by 1 July 2014, with interim stunning requirements, cited over 150 million sheep and cattle exported in 30 years and more than two million deaths en route.

The Queensland floods and Cyclone Yasi prompted debate over the Temporary Flood and Cyclone Reconstruction Levy bills, with speakers recalling the devastation—the worst flooding in history, affecting Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria, and Tasmania, plus fires in Western Australia—and supporting the levy to fund recovery. Opposition senators used the broader debate to accuse the Labor government of incompetence and dishonesty, citing 23 broken promises since 2010, including on the education revolution, trade training centres, GroceryWatch, Fuelwatch, and the carbon tax.
